content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"The Transformer Architecture: Self-Attention and Multi-Head Attention"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Introduced in the landmark 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani et al., the Transformer architecture revolutionized Natural Language Processing (NLP). Unlike previous architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and LSTMs that process text sequentially, Transformers process entire sequences simultaneously, relying entirely on attention mechanisms to model relationships between words."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Limitations of Recurrent Models"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional sequential models suffer from two major bottlenecks: computational inefficiency due to the inability to parallelize training across sequence lengths, and the vanishing gradient problem, which makes it difficult to retain context over long distances. The Transformer resolves these issues by replacing recurrence with self-attention."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"The Core Concept of Self-Attention"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Self-attention allows the model to associate each word in a sentence with every other word, dynamically capturing contextual dependencies regardless of their positional distance. To compute self-attention, every input token is projected into three distinct vectors: Queries (Q), Keys (K), and Values (V)."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Queries (Q): The representation of the current word trying to attend to other words."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keys (K): The representations against which the query is evaluated to determine relevance."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Values (V): The actual content vectors that are aggregated based on the calculated attention weights."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Scaled Dot-Product Attention Formula"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"The attention mechanism is formally defined by the scaled dot-product attention equation:"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( (Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k) ) * V"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, d_k represents the dimensionality of the keys. The scaling factor (1 / sqrt(d_k)) prevents the dot products from growing too large in magnitude, which would otherwise push the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients during backpropagation."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Multi-Head Attention: Expanding Representation Capacity"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Rather than performing a single attention function with d_model-dimensional queries, keys, and values, Multi-Head Attention linearly projects the queries, keys, and values h times with different, learned linear projections. This allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) * W^O\nwhere head_i = Attention(Q * W_i^Q, K * W_i^K, V * W_i^V)"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"By combining scaled dot-product self-attention with multi-head projections, Transformers achieve unprecedented capability in understanding semantic structures in text. This foundation powers modern state-of-the-art models like BERT, GPT-4, and T5."}]
